title: JavaScript first-class functions and EventTarget (JS/TS comparison)
hook: If you think in Node.js callbacks, map them onto C# delegates and events — but do not say C# has first-class functions the way JavaScript does. Methods become values only after you bind them to a delegate type.

blocks.text: In **JavaScript**, every function is an object you can pass, return, and store without a conversion step. In **C#**, a method is not a value until you assign it to a **delegate** (Func, Action, or a custom type). **TypeScript** function types like `(msg: Message) => Promise<void>` check at compile time but erase at runtime. C# delegate types remain in metadata and the Common Language Runtime (CLR) validates invocations.

entries.plainDefinition: A function treated as a value you can assign to variables, pass as arguments, and return from other functions.
The browser and Node API for addEventListener and removeEventListener with string event names.
When a method name appears where a delegate is expected, the compiler converts it if signatures match.

blocks.text: Coming from JavaScript or TypeScript, the mental model shift is the **type boundary**: C# middleware is `List<Func<Message, CancellationToken, Task>>`, not an untyped callback array. EventTarget uses string event names and requires the same function reference to unsubscribe — like C# **-=**, but C# events are typed members, not a runtime registry. Both ecosystems leak if a long-lived emitter holds a short-lived listener.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: Say: JavaScript functions are first-class objects; C# methods become objects as typed delegates. Closest JS analogue to C# events is EventTarget with identical-reference unsubscribe.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Pass a callback
items.body: JS: pass function directly. C#: pass Func/Action or method group converted to delegate.

items.title: Build middleware pipeline
items.body: JS: array of functions you loop. C#: List<Func<...>> or multicast delegate with +=.

items.title: Subscribe to events
items.body: JS: addEventListener(type, fn). C#: publisher.Event += handler on a typed member.

items.title: Unsubscribe
items.body: Both require the same reference. JS AbortSignal or removeEventListener; C# -= or Dispose.

snippet.explanation: Line 2: same function reference subscribed. Line 4: AbortSignal bulk-unsubscribes. C# has no built-in once flag — unsubscribe in the handler or use a disposable wrapper.

blocks.title: Saying C# has first-class functions without mentioning delegates
blocks.body: Methods are not values until converted. Always name Func, Action, or a custom delegate when comparing to JavaScript.

blocks.title: Comparing event to EventEmitter without noting typing
blocks.body: Node EventEmitter uses string event names. C# events are compile-time members with a fixed delegate signature.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: when comparing a Node EventEmitter fan-out to C# multicast, both skip later listeners on throw unless you wrap each call — log listener index in both stacks to confirm. TypeScript function types erase at runtime; a wrong callback shape fails only at call time. C# delegate mismatch is a compile error. For cross-language teams, document that C# requires Func/Action at API boundaries, not raw method groups passed like JS callbacks.

snippet.label: JS-style listener array versus C# multicast exception semantics
snippet.explanation: Line 6: C# multicast matches JS listener arrays for ordering and exception behavior. Line 9: explicit isolation is required in both ecosystems for fault-tolerant fan-out.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying C# has first-class functions like JavaScript without naming delegates. Comparing C# events to EventEmitter string names without noting compile-time typing. Not knowing multicast exception behavior is identical unless you isolate each handler.

interviewTakeaways: JavaScript functions are first-class objects; C# methods become values only through delegate conversion.
EventTarget and C# events both require the same reference for unsubscribe; multicast exception skips later handlers in both.
TypeScript function types erase at runtime; C# delegate types are enforced by the CLR on every invoke.
60s: JS passes functions natively. C# needs Func/Action/delegate. Events are typed members, not string names. Multicast exception same in both — isolate per handler. TS types gone at runtime.
Follow-up: how does AbortSignal in JS map to IDisposable unsubscribe in C#?
commonPitfalls: Saying C# has first-class functions without mentioning the delegate type.
Comparing event to Node EventEmitter's string names without noting the typed member.
Assuming removeEventListener('message', () => {}) works — it does not, for the same reason -= new lambda fails.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Pass, return, and store functions freely. C# stores Func/Action/custom delegates instead of raw method tokens.
addEventListener/removeEventListener with identical references; AbortSignal for lifetime. Map this to event += / -= and IDisposable.
